intro: IELTS Reading matnni ko'chirib yozishni emas, MA'NONI tanishni tekshiradi. Shuning uchun savolda bir so'z, matnda esa uning sinonimi turadi. Bu — paraphrase.
Misol: savolda "friendly inhabitants", matnda "friendlier populations". "Inhabitants" va "populations" — bir ma'no, boshqa so'z.
Qoida: SAVOLNI o'zgartirmang, MATNNI qidiring. Avval savoldan kalit so'zni belgilang (ot, fe'l, raqam, ism), keyin matndan o'sha ma'noni qidiring.
Javobni yozganda esa aksincha: javob MATNDAGI so'z bilan yoziladi. O'zingizning sinonimingiz — noto'g'ri javob.

4 xil paraphrase: 1) sinonim (money — cash); 2) so'z turkumi o'zgaradi (relaxed lifestyle — a relaxed way of life); 3) antonim + inkor (have less money — don't have so much money); 4) umumiy so'z (Rio, Lilongwe — cities).
Ism, raqam, sana va joy nomlari paraphrase qilinmaydi — ular matnda xuddi o'sha holda turadi. Shuning uchun ular eng tez topiladigan "langar" (anchor) hisoblanadi.
formulas: "People don't have so much ___" — kalit: don't have so much
Bo'sh joydan oldingi va keyingi so'zga qarang
don't have so much = have less
Rio de Janeiro, 93 percent — ism va raqam o'zgarmaydi
Faqat bir so'zni emas, butun gapni
presentation: Savolda "friendly inhabitants" bor, matnda bu so'z yo'q. Nima qilaman?
Sinonimini qidiraman: "friendlier populations". Inhabitants = populations.
Javobni o'z so'zim bilan yozsam bo'ladimi?
Yo'q. Table completion javobi matndagi so'z bilan, xuddi o'sha shaklda yoziladi.
Matnda "relaxed way of life", savolda "relaxed ___ lifestyle" — qaysi biri javob?
Javob — matndagi so'z: bu yerda savolga "lifestyle" mos keladi, chunki "way of life" = lifestyle.
Ism va raqamlarni ham paraphrase qilishadimi?
Yo'q. Rio, Amsterdam, 93% — o'zgarmaydi. Shuning uchun ulardan boshlab qidiring.
Bir so'z so'ralganda "a lot of money" deb yozsam?
Noto'g'ri. ONE WORD ONLY — faqat "money".
Matnni boshidan oxirigacha o'qiymanmi?
Yo'q. Table completion javoblari matnda TARTIB bilan keladi — savol tartibida qidiring.
notes: Bu birinchi dars: o'quvchilarga "IELTSda javob matnda turadi, faqat boshqa so'z bilan" degan fikrni mahkam o'rnating.
Har javobdan keyin SO'RANG: "matndagi qaysi so'z savoldagi so'zga teng?" — javobni emas, yo'lni tekshiring.
Xatolar daftarining birinchi sahifasi shu darsda ochiladi: chap ustun "savolda", o'ng ustun "matnda".
Vaqt: har qo'shimcha matnga 8 daqiqa (IELTSda 1 passage ≈ 20 daqiqa, bu qisqartirilgan mashq).
mistakes: Javobni o'z sinonimi bilan yozish (matn "money", o'quvchi "cash")
So'z chegarasini buzish ("so much money" — 2 so'z)
ONE WORD ONLY yozuvi savol ustida turadi
Faqat kalit so'zni ko'rib, gapni o'qimaslik
Bir so'z bir nechta joyda uchraydi, ma'no gapda ochiladi
Matn deyarli har doim boshqa so'z ishlatadi

readings.title: The city that pays you to live there
text: In 2019, the small town of Candela in southern Italy had a problem. Young people were leaving for the big cities, and only about 2,700 residents remained. Shops closed, the school lost half its pupils, and the streets were quiet even in summer. So the mayor tried something unusual: he offered money to anyone who moved there. A single person received 800 euros, a couple 1,200 euros, and a family with children up to 2,000 euros. The only conditions were that newcomers had to rent or buy a house in the town and find work that paid at least 7,500 euros a year.

The idea worked better than anyone expected. Within a year, more than fifty families had applied, and the town hall received phone calls from as far away as Brazil. Candela is not rich, but it is safe, the air is clean, and a two-bedroom flat costs less than a parking space in Milan. For families with small children, that difference matters more than a high salary.

Other places have copied the plan. In Japan, the government of a mountain village gives free land to anyone who builds a house and stays for ten years. In Spain, the village of Ponga pays 3,000 euros to each couple who moves in, plus 3,000 more for every baby born there. Officials in these places say the aim is not tourism but population: a village without children has no future.

Not everyone is convinced. Critics point out that money brings people for a year or two, but only jobs keep them. In Candela, about a third of the new arrivals left again when their contracts ended. The mayor agrees, but he says the town is still better off than before: the school has reopened its second class, and two cafés now stay open until midnight.

readings.title: Where the streets have no cars
text: Pontevedra is a medium-sized city in the north-west of Spain. Thirty years ago its narrow streets were full of traffic: about 14,000 cars passed through the old centre every day, the air was dirty, and between 1990 and 1996 thirty people died in road accidents. In 1999 a new mayor, who had worked as a doctor, decided that the centre belonged to people rather than to vehicles. Cars were not banned, but parking in the middle of the city was removed, speed limits were cut to 30 kilometres an hour, and pavements were widened.

The results surprised the rest of Europe. Traffic in the centre fell by around 90 per cent, and carbon dioxide emissions dropped by two thirds. Since 2011 nobody has been killed in a traffic accident inside the city. Shops, which had been afraid of losing customers, now report more visitors, because people who walk stop more often than people who drive.

The city also changed the way children travel to school. A scheme called "Metrominuto" gives every family a map that looks like an underground railway map, but the coloured lines show walking routes and the time each journey takes: eight minutes from the market to the town hall, twelve minutes from the station to the park. Today about seven out of ten children walk to school without an adult, a figure almost unknown in other European cities.

Pontevedra is not perfect. Some older residents complain that deliveries are slower, and drivers from nearby villages say they must park far from the shops. Yet the population of the centre has grown by 12,000 since the changes began, while many other Spanish old towns have emptied.

readings.title: The quietest city in the world
text: Noise is not only unpleasant; it is dangerous. The World Health Organization says that long periods of loud sound raise blood pressure, damage sleep and, in European cities, shorten thousands of lives every year. Anything above 65 decibels during the day is considered harmful. A busy road reaches about 80 decibels, and a motorcycle passing close by reaches 95.

For this reason a number of cities now measure noise as carefully as they measure air pollution. Zurich, in Switzerland, is usually named the quietest large city in Europe. Its trams run on rubber-covered rails, rubbish is collected before seven in the morning only in the outer districts, and building work must stop at eight in the evening. Residents can report noise through a mobile application, and the city answers within 48 hours.

The opposite example is often said to be Dhaka, the capital of Bangladesh, where the average street noise reaches 119 decibels — louder than a rock concert. Most of it comes from car horns. Drivers use the horn as a greeting, a warning and a complaint, sometimes more than a thousand times an hour on a single street. In 2020 the government tried a "no horn" day; the noise fell by only 5 per cent, because most drivers ignored it.

Solutions do exist, and they are cheaper than people expect. Trees along a road cut noise by up to 10 decibels. Rubber road surfaces cut it by 5. In South Korea, some flats now have "quiet floors" made of thick material, after complaints between neighbours became one of the most common reasons for arguments in the whole country.
paraphrases: the example that shows the other side

readings.title: The country that measures happiness instead of money
text: Most governments judge success by one number: how much the economy grows each year. Bhutan, a small kingdom in the Himalayas with about 780,000 people, does something different. Since 1972 it has used a measure called Gross National Happiness, and in 2008 this idea was written into the country's new constitution.

The measure has four main parts: fair economic development, protection of the environment, care for culture, and good government. Every few years officials visit homes across the country and ask each family a long list of questions. The survey takes around three hours per household and covers thirty-three indicators, from sleep and health to trust in neighbours.

The environmental rule is the strictest in the world. The constitution says that at least 60 per cent of the land must stay under forest for ever; today the real figure is about 71 per cent. Because the forests absorb more carbon than the country produces, Bhutan is one of the few carbon-negative nations on Earth.

The system has problems too. Young people leave for Australia and India, where salaries are five or six times higher, and unemployment among graduates reached 29 per cent in 2022. Critics say happiness is difficult to measure and easy to use in advertising. Officials answer that no number is perfect, but a country that counts only money will protect only money.

readings.title: The library that lends everything except books
text: In the Canadian city of Toronto there is a library where the shelves hold no novels. Instead, members borrow tools: drills, ladders, sewing machines, tents and even musical instruments. The Toronto Tool Library opened in 2013 with 150 tools donated by local families. Today it holds more than 10,000 items and has about 5,000 members, who pay a yearly fee of 50 dollars.

The idea is simple. An electric drill is used, on average, for only thirteen minutes in its entire life, yet almost every household owns one. Sharing a single drill among fifty families saves money and space, and it also cuts waste: fewer machines are built, and fewer are thrown away.

Similar libraries have opened in more than 500 cities worldwide. In Berlin, one branch lends camping equipment; in Melbourne, another lends party supplies such as tables and lights. The most popular item almost everywhere is the pressure washer, which is expensive to buy and needed perhaps twice a year.

Running such a library is harder than it looks. Tools break, and repairs take up a quarter of the budget. Some members keep items too long, so most branches now charge a small fine for every day an item is late. Staff also teach short courses — how to fix a bicycle, how to use a saw safely — and these classes bring in nearly half of the income at the Toronto branch.

readings.title: Living on a floating island
text: Lake Titicaca lies between Peru and Bolivia, 3,812 metres above sea level. On the Peruvian side live the Uros people, whose homes stand on about 120 artificial islands made entirely of totora, a reed that grows in the shallow water near the shore.

Building an island takes a community around one year. First, blocks of root and soil are cut from the lake bed and tied together with rope; these blocks float because they contain gas. Reeds are then laid on top in layers, each layer crossing the one below. A finished island is roughly two metres thick, but the surface reed rots quickly, so fresh reeds must be added every two weeks in the rainy season.

Life on the islands has changed. Fifty years ago most families lived by fishing and hunting birds. Today around 2,000 people live on the islands and most income comes from tourism: nearly 200,000 visitors arrive each year, and many islands now have solar panels, which power lights and a television. The largest island has a school, a small hospital and a radio station.

There are worries. Young Uros often move to the city of Puno for work or study, and the reed beds are shrinking because of warmer water and pollution. A local guide explains the problem simply: the islands survive only while somebody keeps adding reeds.

lessons.title: Listening: Form Completion (Section 1)
lessons.book_ref: Coursebook: Unit 1, Listening (Form completion), 10-bet, 1–5-mashqlar, Audio 01–03 ("Dubai Palm Apartments"). Workbook: Unit 1, Listening (Form completion), 8-bet. Kitob audiosi va skripti kitobda — bu yerda uchta mustaqil skript to'liq transkripti bilan berilgan.
objectives: Section 1 dagi formani to'ldirishda javob turini oldindan aniqlash (ism, raqam, sana, narx).
Harflab aytilgan ism va familiyani (spelling) va telefon raqamini xatosiz yozish.
Raqam, sana, pul va vaqtni IELTS qoidasi bo'yicha yozish.
"Tuzatish" (correction) holatini eshitish: so'zlovchi javobni o'zgartirganda oxirgisini olish.
So'z chegarasini bajarish: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER.
materials: Bu rejadagi 3 ta skript: ustoz o'qiydi yoki audio qo'yiladi
Har o'quvchida forma nusxasi va qalam
Harflar jadvali: shunga o'xshash tovushlar (B/P, M/N, S/F, G/J, I/E)
timeline: Salomlashish, o'tgan darsdagi savol turini 3 savolda eslatish
Ustoz doskada: qoida, bosqichlar, tipik xatolar
Kitobdagi topshiriq birga bajariladi, har javob izohlanadi
Matndagi va savoldagi so'zlar jadvali; o'quvchilar ovoz chiqarib topadi
Mustaqil bajariladi, keyin javoblar izoh bilan tekshiriladi
Skript ustoz tomonidan o'qiladi yoki audio qo'yiladi, keyin transkript bilan tekshiriladi

intro: Section 1 — telefon suhbati yoki ro'yxatdan o'tish. Javoblar deyarli har doim: ism, familiya, manzil, telefon, sana, narx, vaqt.
Formani eshitishdan OLDIN o'qing va har bo'sh joy ustiga turini yozing: N (name), NUM (number), D (date), $ (price), T (time).
Ism va manzil harflab aytiladi. Faqat harflarni yozing, keyin so'zga aylantiring. B–P, M–N, S–F, G–J, I–E — eng ko'p adashtiradigan juftlar.
Telefon raqamida "double" = ikkita bir xil raqam (double four = 44), "oh" yoki "zero" = 0.
Javob TUZATILISHI mumkin: "It's 15 Park Road — sorry, 50 Park Road". To'g'ri javob — oxirgisi.
So'z chegarasi: "TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER" bo'lsa, "50 Park Road" (2 so'z + raqam) mumkin, "the 50 Park Road" — yo'q.
Audio BIR MARTA qo'yiladi. Javobni yozib, darhol keyingi bo'sh joyga o'ting; orqaga qaytish yo'q.
presentation: "Double seven two six" — qanday yoziladi?
7726. "Double" ikkita bir xil raqamni bildiradi.
So'zlovchi "B for Bravo" desa?
Bu harfni aniqlashtirish. Faqat B harfini yozasiz.
Sana qanday yoziladi?
9 January, 9th January yoki January 9 — hammasi qabul qilinadi.
Narx "maximum 60 euros" bo'lsa, javobga nima yoziladi?
Formada "euros" bo'lsa, faqat 60. Aks holda "60 euros".
Javobni eshitib ulgurmadim, nima qilay?
Bo'sh qoldiring va keyingisiga o'ting. Bitta javob uchun ikkitasini yo'qotmang.
"Fifteen" va "fifty" ni qanday farqlayman?
Urg'uga qarang: FIFteen (boshida), fifTY (oxirida). Shubha bo'lsa, kontekst yordam beradi.
notes: Kitob audiosi (01–03) bo'lsa — avval o'sha, keyin bu yerdagi skriptlar. Audio bo'lmasa, ustoz skriptni tabiiy tezlikda BIR MARTA o'qiydi.
Ustoz o'qiyotganda transkriptni o'quvchilarga ko'rsatmaydi; tekshiruvdan keyin ochiladi.
Har skriptdan keyin: "qaysi so'z javobga olib keldi?" — signal so'zni toping (so, that's, let me repeat).
Imlo xatosi = 0 ball. Shuning uchun harflab yozish mashqi har darsda 2 daqiqa takrorlanadi.
mistakes: Ism har doim bosh harf bilan
Formadagi mavjud so'zni takrorlash ("60 euros" bo'lsa "euros" yozish)

listenings.title: Student accommodation office
listenings.audios: Jony Academy skripti — ustoz o'qiydi yoki yozib olinadi
intro: Ariza formasi: talaba turar joy so'rab qo'ng'iroq qilmoqda. BIR MARTA tinglang.
Ko'rsatma: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
transcript: OFFICER: Good morning, City College Accommodation Office. How can I help you?
STUDENT: Hello. I'd like to find a room for the next semester, please.
OFFICER: Of course. Can I take your name?
STUDENT: Yes, it's Daniela Oster.
OFFICER: Could you spell the surname for me?
STUDENT: O-S-T-E-R. Oster.
OFFICER: Thank you. And where are you from, Daniela?
STUDENT: I'm from Austria, from Graz.
OFFICER: Lovely. What are you studying?
STUDENT: Architecture. It's a two-year master's course.
OFFICER: And your student number?
STUDENT: It's 4-0-double 2-7. Four zero two two seven.
OFFICER: 40227, thank you. Now, what kind of accommodation are you looking for?
STUDENT: A single room, if possible. I shared last year and I couldn't study.
OFFICER: Right, a single room. And when would you like to move in?
STUDENT: The 3rd of September. Actually, sorry — make that the 10th of September. My flight changed.
OFFICER: The 10th of September. How long do you want the room for?
STUDENT: Nine months, until June.
OFFICER: And your budget? Rooms start at about 400 pounds a month.
STUDENT: I can pay up to 550 a month, but not more.
OFFICER: That's fine. Any special requirements?
STUDENT: Two things. I'd like a room with a desk — a proper one, not a small table. And I need somewhere close to the library, because I work late.
OFFICER: Near the library, noted. Do you need parking?
STUDENT: No, I don't drive. But I have a bicycle, so somewhere to keep it would help.
OFFICER: We have bike storage at most buildings. Finally, a contact number?
STUDENT: My mobile is 07-double 4-9 3-1-5-2-6.
OFFICER: 07449 31526. I'll email you three options this afternoon.

tasks.type: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
why: "I'm from Austria, from Graz". Mamlakat so'ralgan, shahar emas.
"A single room, if possible". Bitta so'z yetarli.
Avval 3-sentabr aytilgan, keyin tuzatilgan: "make that the 10th".
"I can pay up to 550 a month". 400 — eng past narx, talab emas.
"I'd like a room with a desk".
"I have a bicycle, so somewhere to keep it".

listenings.title: Sports centre membership
intro: Sport markaziga a'zo bo'lish uchun qo'ng'iroq. BIR MARTA tinglang, keyin transkript bilan tekshiring.
transcript: RECEPTIONIST: Riverside Sports Centre, good afternoon.
CALLER: Hi. I'd like to join the centre, please.
RECEPTIONIST: Certainly. I'll take a few details. Your full name?
CALLER: Peter Vaughan.
RECEPTIONIST: How do you spell Vaughan?
CALLER: V-A-U-G-H-A-N.
RECEPTIONIST: Thank you. And your address?
CALLER: It's 16 Ashgrove Lane — that's A-S-H-G-R-O-V-E — in Newport.
RECEPTIONIST: 16 Ashgrove Lane, Newport. Postcode?
CALLER: NP19 7TB.
RECEPTIONIST: And your date of birth?
CALLER: The 12th of March, 1996.
RECEPTIONIST: Which membership would you like? We have standard, which is gym only, and full, which includes the pool and all classes.
CALLER: What's the difference in price?
RECEPTIONIST: Standard is 28 pounds a month; full is 41.
CALLER: I'll take the full one. I mainly want to swim.
RECEPTIONIST: Good choice. Students get 20 per cent off, by the way. Are you a student?
CALLER: Not any more, I finished in June.
RECEPTIONIST: Fine. Which day would you like to start?
CALLER: Can I start on Monday the 1st?
RECEPTIONIST: Yes, the 1st of October is fine. Do you have any medical conditions we should know about?
CALLER: I had a knee operation two years ago, so no running classes for me.
RECEPTIONIST: I'll note that. And how did you hear about us?
CALLER: A friend at work recommended you. Actually, I also saw your advert on the radio.
RECEPTIONIST: I'll put "friend". Last thing: an emergency contact.
CALLER: My sister, Karen. Her number is 0-7-8-double 3-1-4-2-9.
RECEPTIONIST: 07883 1429... sorry, could you repeat the last four?
CALLER: One four two nine.
RECEPTIONIST: Got it. Your card will be ready on Thursday.

listenings.title: Taxi booking for the airport
intro: Taksi buyurtmasi. Uyda bir marta tinglang (yoki oila a'zosi o'qib bersin), keyin transkript bilan tekshiring.
transcript: OPERATOR: Blue Line Taxis, how can I help?
CUSTOMER: I'd like to book a taxi to the airport, please.
OPERATOR: Certainly. Which airport?
CUSTOMER: Stansted.
OPERATOR: And the pick-up address?
CUSTOMER: 8 Chandler Street. C-H-A-N-D-L-E-R.
OPERATOR: 8 Chandler Street. What date do you need it?
CUSTOMER: The 23rd of April, next Tuesday.
OPERATOR: And what time?
CUSTOMER: My flight is at 9.40 in the morning, so I should leave at about half past five.
OPERATOR: We recommend leaving three and a half hours before, so 6.10 would be enough. But if you prefer 5.30, that's fine.
CUSTOMER: Let's say 5.45, in the middle.
OPERATOR: 5.45 it is. How many passengers?
CUSTOMER: Three adults and one child.
OPERATOR: Any luggage?
CUSTOMER: Four large suitcases, so we'll need the big car.
OPERATOR: That's the estate, which costs 65 pounds to Stansted. The normal car is 48, but it won't take four cases.
CUSTOMER: The estate, then.
OPERATOR: Do you want to pay by card now or cash on the day?
CUSTOMER: Card, please. Actually no — cash is easier, I'll pay the driver.
OPERATOR: Cash it is. Your name and mobile?
CUSTOMER: Amira Haddad. H-A-double D-A-D. And my number is 07-9-double 6-2-0-1-3-4.
OPERATOR: 07996 20134, thank you. The driver will text you ten minutes before he arrives.
